# Expert Question 1 (Round 1) — Framing the core teamwork model

## Current understanding
MM-Bench 2020_D: build a passing network from 23,429 Huskies/opponent passes across
38 matches (30 Huskies, 19 opponents x2) and quantify structural + dynamical
features of teamwork; identify performance indicators beyond goals/wins; give the
coach structural-strategy advice for next season; generalize to team design.

Season context (matches.csv): 14 W / 11 L / 13 T, 32 goals for / 58 against; the
coach changed at match 10 (Coach1 -> Coach2 -> Coach3), and the record improved
sharply under Coach3 (11 of the last 15 matches unlost, most wins of the season
with the last coach).

The provided literature (Buldú et al. 2018, Front. Psychol. 9:1900) supplies the
empirical baseline: soccer passing networks are small-world (clustering far above
Erdős–Rényi null at equal n, m, path length comparable), degree distribution
heavy-tailed, and betweenness-centrality-based team metrics correlate with win
probability; network centroid/stretch/entropy also track performance.

## Decision point
How should the **core teamwork model** (subtask 2: "a model that captures
structural, configurational, and dynamical aspects of teamwork") be formulated?
The network-analysis subtasks are standard, but the modeling framework has major
downstream impact on the whole report.

## Candidate strategies

**A. Descriptive indicator suite + small-world null-model validation +
regression on match outcome (recommended).**
Build weighted directed passing networks at micro/meso/macro scales and short/long
time scales; define teamwork indicators (dyadic reciprocity, triadic clustering
coefficients, degree/assortativity, betweenness/closeness centrality, hub
concentration, network centroid & stretch, pass-type diversity, pass-sequence
entropy, minute-to-minute tempo variability, contribution distribution
[Gini/Spearman], first-vs-second-half shifts, coach/era comparison). Validate
against ER and degree-preserving null models; test association with outcome via
per-match multivariate regression / simple logistic model with a holdout.
- Advantages: directly matches literature baseline; every indicator is checkable
  against win/loss; robust and reproducible with 38 matches; yields concrete
  structural advice.
- Limitations: correlational, small per-opponent sample (n=2 games/opponent);
  indicators are descriptive rather than mechanistic.

**B. Generative / mechanistic agent-based model of the team.**
Simulate player positions and a passing-choice rule conditioned on network
parameters, calibrate to reproduce observed dyad/triad frequencies, then test
which parameter changes improve simulated "success".
- Advantages: mechanistic; can do counterfactuals ("what if we rebalance passes?").
- Limitations: heavy engineering for this data volume and 38-match calibration
  set; pass *completeness* is unobserved (only completed passes are logged), so a
  generative pass-completion model would require inventing failed passes; high
  risk of overfitting.

**C. Stochastic-block / latent-dynamic community model as the core.**
Model the season as a time-varying stochastic block structure with latent
formation states; treat "teamwork quality" as the block structure's stability.
- Advantages: explicitly "configurational"; clean dynamical story across the
  season and coach changes.
- Limitations: 30 players with only ~4–6 passes per dyad per game makes latent
  class identification fragile; inference is complex and conclusions harder to
  validate; weaker direct link to the win-probability evidence in the literature.

I recommend **A**, with a lightweight B-style counterfactual (reweighting
existing edges, re-simulating indicators) used *only* to sanity-check the
structural advice in subtask 3, and C's community-detection results reported as
part of the descriptive suite rather than as the core model.

## Impact
This choice fixes which indicators must be built, which validation is performed,
and what the coach-facing recommendations and the generalization section (subtask
4) are based on.

# Expert Question 2 (Round 2) — Outcome-linkage strategy under severe underpowering

## Understanding after Round 1
Confirmed framework A: three-layer descriptive suite (structural / configurational /
dynamical), each indicator validated against ER and degree-preserving nulls,
regressed on per-match outcome with a holdout; B-style edge reweighting only as
counterfactual sanity check; community detection reported descriptively.

## Decision point
The outcome linkage is badly underpowered: 38 matches, ~20 candidate indicators,
and 19 opponents played exactly twice (per-opponent effects unusable). A naive
38-sample regression over 20 indicators cannot be validated and would be
overfitting theater. How should I link indicators to outcome so the claim "these
indicators reflect successful teamwork" is defensible?

## Candidate strategies

**S1. Aggregation + staged univariate screening + small penalized multivariate
model (recommended).**
(a) Aggregate to 3 levels: per-match (n=38), per-coach-era (Coach1: 9, Coach2: 5,
Coach3: 24; also pre/post-match-10 = 9/29), per-season. Run the indicator suite at
all three.
(b) For each indicator: paired comparison of wins vs non-wins (or wins vs losses)
with exact/permutation p-values — permutation keeps validity under n=38 and
correlated observations.
(c) Take only indicators significant at a controlled FDR (BH, q<0.20, relaxed for
power) into a *single* small multivariate model: logistic regression with
L1/L2 penalty (or ridge + forward stepwise), validated by leave-one-match-out
cross-validation and permutation; report effect sizes, not p-values, as primary
evidence.
(d) Report the coach-era comparison (Coach3 vs Coach1) as the main "what changed
worked" story since n=24 vs 9 has some power on the strongest indicators.
- Advantages: honest about power; permutation/FDR keep claims defensible;
  effect sizes + era contrast give the coach a clear narrative; cheap to compute.
- Limitations: correlation ≠ causation; era contrast conflates coach change with
  season progression; FDR at q=0.20 means borderline evidence.

**S2. Pure univariate, no multivariate model.**
Screen each indicator alone (permutation tests), report a table of effect sizes;
skip the joint model entirely.
- Advantages: simplest, no overfit risk.
- Limitations: weaker "model that captures teamwork" story (subtask 2 asks for a
  *model*); ignores indicator redundancy (many indicators are correlated: e.g.
  degree heterogeneity ~ hub concentration ~ betweenness balance).

**S3. Dimensionality reduction (PCA) on the indicator matrix, then regress
outcome on the first few PCs.**
- Advantages: shrinks to few uncorrelated axes; defensible at n=38.
- Limitations: PCs are hard to translate into coach advice; the "model" becomes a
  black box; interpretability of subtask 3 suffers.

## Impact
Fixes the validation design (permutation scheme, FDR level, multivariate model
and its CV) and determines which indicators become "the ones that matter" in the
coach advice and generalization sections.

# Expert Question 3 (Round 3) — Network topology conventions

## Understanding after Rounds 1–2
Framework A (three-layer indicator suite, null-validated, S1 outcome linkage) is
fixed. Before building subtask 1's network, one decision determines the topology
of every network quantity (dyadic/triadic configurations, clustering, centrality,
community structure) and therefore everything downstream.

## Decision point
The dataset contains passes by *both* teams (Huskies and each opponent; 366
players total). "Create a network for the ball passing between players" could be
read several ways. Which node/link convention should be canonical?

## Candidate strategies

**N1. Huskies-only nodes, intra-Huskies passes only (recommended), reported as the
primary network.**
Nodes = 30 Huskies players; link (i→j) weight = number of completed Huskies-to-
Huskies passes. Opponent passes used only (a) to define match outcome/context and
(b) for a short "oppressor network" comparison of how opponents' structures
differ from the Huskies' (e.g. when the Huskies win, does the opponent network
fragment?).
- Advantages: matches the coach's question (Huskies teamwork); ~30 nodes and a
  clean player roster; player-position structure (G/D/M/F) directly interpretable;
  literature baseline (Buldú et al.) is built exactly this way (team passing
  networks).
- Limitations: excludes through-balls to opponents / long balls intercepted —
  but passingevents.csv only contains *completed* passes, so cross-team edges are
  rarely observed anyway; needs a quick count to confirm.

**N2. Full match network: all 20–22 players on the pitch per match, both teams,
  cross-team passes included when present.**
- Advantages: captures "interactions between players" literally; can study
  how opponents break Huskies patterns (subtask 3's "dependent on
  opponents' counter-strategies" angle).
- Limitations: nodes/links mix two teams, so clustering, reciprocity and
  centrality conflate intra- and inter-team play; per-player identities
  (OpponentX_F1) are anonymous across matches; harder to link to Huskies
  coaching decisions; the "network" the coach asked about is no longer the
  Huskies' network.

**N3. Hybrid: N1 primary + per-position aggregate (G/D/M/F × 2-3) secondary.**
Collapse the 30 players to ~8–10 position-group nodes for formation-level
readings (e.g. "how does G→M→F flow shift between eras?"), alongside N1.
- Advantages: robust to small per-player pass counts (some players have very few
  passes); directly answers "team formations"; still N1 at the player level.
- Limitations: extra bookkeeping; position groups conflate players of the same
  role.

My recommendation: **N1 as the canonical network** (all dyadic/triadic,
centrality, community, and outcome-linked indicators computed on it), **N3's
position-group aggregation as a secondary formation layer**, and a compact
**N2-style opponent-structure contrast** (opponent-network density/clustering vs
Huskies, wins vs losses) to answer the "opponent-dependent strategies" clause.

## Impact
Fixes the node set, edge definition, and how opponent data is used, so the whole
indicator suite in Rounds 1–2 is computed on a well-defined network.
expert_answers:
**Formulate the core model as A: a descriptive, multi-scale indicator suite validated against null models and linked to match outcome by regression.**

Rationale: the data support only completed passes, so a mechanistic model (B) would require inventing unobserved failures, and 30 players with few passes per dyad make latent-block inference (C) fragile. A yields indicators that are directly checkable against win/loss and coach eras, matching the Buldú et al. baseline.

Structure it in three layers: (1) structural — weighted directed passing networks at micro/meso/macro scales; (2) configurational — dyadic reciprocity, triadic clustering, community/formation blocks, centrality and hub concentration; (3) dynamical — tempo variability, pass-sequence entropy, half-to-half and season-long shifts.

Validate each indicator against Erdős–Rényi and degree-preserving nulls, then regress per-match outcome on the indicator set with a holdout. Use B-style edge reweighting only as a counterfactual sanity check, and report C's community detection within the descriptive suite.

**Use S1: aggregation + staged univariate screening + a small penalized multivariate model.**

Rationale: S2 undercuts subtask 2's demand for a *model* and ignores indicator redundancy; S3's PCs are uninterpretable for coach advice. S1 is the only option that stays honest under n=38 while still producing a defensible joint model.

Concretely: run the suite at per-match, per-era, and per-season levels; screen each indicator by permutation test on wins vs non-wins; carry only FDR-surviving indicators (BH, q<0.20) into one penalized logistic model validated by leave-one-match-out CV and permutation. Report effect sizes as primary evidence, p-values as secondary. Treat the Coach3-vs-Coach1 era contrast as the headline narrative, explicitly flagged as confounded with season progression.

**Adopt N1 as canonical, with N3's position-group layer as secondary and a compact N2-style opponent contrast.**

Rationale: the coach's question is about Huskies teamwork, and the Buldú et al. baseline is built on single-team passing networks, so N1 keeps every downstream quantity (dyadic/triadic configurations, clustering, centrality, community structure) interpretable and comparable to the literature. N2 as primary would conflate intra- and inter-team play in every topological measure and lose per-player identity across matches. N3's G/D/M/F aggregation is worth adding only as a formation-level secondary reading, since some players have too few passes for stable per-player statistics. The opponent-network contrast (density/clustering vs Huskies, wins vs losses) is the right minimal use of opponent data to address the opponent-dependent-strategies clause, without contaminating the primary network.
